analysis.one_liner: Bans health insurers from gagging doctors, secret bonuses that reward limiting care, and clauses that shield insurers from lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to three House committees and their subcommittees, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have stopped health insurance companies from putting clauses in contracts that prevent doctors from telling patients about treatment options or speaking publicly about care decisions. It would have banned bonus plans that pay doctors for limiting patient care unless they met the stricter Medicare rules, and outlawed contract clauses letting insurers off the hook when patients or doctors sue them. It also required insurers to disclose in plain English what services are covered, how claims get denied, and any doctor bonus plans, with fines up to $100,000 per violation and the right for patients to sue.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients in managed care and other health plans, who would learn what their plan covers and how it makes decisions, and whose doctors could no longer be contractually silenced or paid to limit care. Doctors also gain: they could freely discuss treatment options and would no longer have to indemnify insurers against lawsuits.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits 'gag rule' contract clauses that stop doctors from telling patients about care options or communicating with the public, with limited exceptions for trade secrets and knowing misrepresentation [S3].

Bans incentive plans that pay providers in ways that could limit patient services unless the plans meet Medicare's physician incentive plan requirements, which restrict paying doctors to withhold care [S2][S3].
Prohibits indemnification clauses under which enrollees or providers must cover the insurer's own liability for damage it caused [S2][S3].
Requires plain-English disclosure of all covered services and limits, the procedures used to approve or deny care, and any doctor incentive plans [S2][S3].
Enforces the rules with civil penalties up to $25,000 per violation (up to $100,000 for repeat violators) and gives anyone aggrieved a private right to sue [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and managed care companies, which would face new contract restrictions, disclosure obligations, federal fines, and lawsuits from patients and doctors.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and managed care plans

drawbacks.text: The bill applies Medicare's incentive-plan rules to far more than Medicare — its definitions reach workers' compensation and auto medical insurance — which insurers could argue imposes a complex federal compliance burden across unrelated lines of business [S3].
A private right of action plus penalties of up to $25,000-$100,000 per violation would invite litigation against insurers, a cost honest supporters would acknowledge could show up in premiums [S3].
The gag-clause ban excepts trade secrets, so insurers could still classify some utilization-review practices as proprietary and shield them from disclosure [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients, the core protections — being told about treatment options, knowing what is covered and how care gets denied, and not having doctors financially rewarded for withholding care — address real harms documented in the managed-care era, and the compliance costs to insurers are the price of those protections. The design is broad: sweeping workers' compensation and auto medical coverage into a Medicare-style regime, and pairing steep fines with a private right of action, would predictably raise insurer litigation and compliance costs, some of which could be passed into premiums. On balance it is a pro-patient bill whose benefits to enrollees outweigh its design flaws.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees and then to subcommittees, where it sat without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote until the Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Rep. Bernard Sanders introduced the bill on March 29, 1996, joined by Reps. Stark, McKinney, Dellums, Hilliard, and Frazer [S1][S3].
The Speaker referred it to the Commerce Committee and also to Ways and Means and Economic and Educational Opportunities, splitting it across three committees [S1][S5].
Within three weeks it was further referred to the Commerce Subcommittee on Health, the Health and Environment Subcommittee, and the Employer-Employee Relations Subcommittee [S5].
No committee reported the bill, no vote ever occurred in either chamber, and its last recorded action was the April 19, 1996 subcommittee referral [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Managed care insurers kept the status quo: gag clauses, doctor bonus plans that reward limiting care, and indemnification clauses remained legal, with no federal penalties or disclosure requirements. Patients gained nothing from this Congress on these issues.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers kept the status quo

for.name: Bernard Sanders
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill banning gag clauses, improper incentive plans, and indemnification clauses in health insurance contracts.

for.name: 9 of 204 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Stark, McKinney, Dellums, Hilliard, and Frazer as original cosponsors.

against.name: House committee chairs (Commerce, Ways and Means, Economic and Educational Opportunities)
against.role: Chairs of the three committees of referral
against.what_they_did: Their committees received the bill in March 1996 and never reported it out; no hearing or markup was held, keeping it off the House floor.

against.name: Managed care and health insurance industry
against.role: Insurers and HMOs offering managed care plans nationwide
against.what_they_did: Would have been the regulated party; the bill's restrictions on gag clauses, provider bonuses, and liability shields targeted standard managed-care contract practices.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll calls exist; its sponsor was an Independent and all ten cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent sponsor's allies, with no Republican support on record [S4].

industries.industry: Health insurers and managed care companies (HMOs)
industries.note: The bill bans three standard managed-care contract tools — doctor gag clauses, bonus plans that reward limiting care, and clauses shielding insurers from their own liability — and adds fines up to $100,000 per violation plus patient lawsuits. Its interest in stopping the bill ran directly against patients' interest in disclosure and full communication with their doctors.

industries.industry: Physicians and other health care providers
industries.note: Doctors could no longer be contractually silenced about treatment options and would no longer be required to cover an insurer's own legal liability. Their interest here ran alongside patients'.
